sections.title: Description
sections.summary: Alternatives on difficult ground: bypass it, remove and replace it, design for it, or modify it. Ground modification is the alteration of site foundation conditions or project earth structures for better performance (USACE 1999), with ten primary functions; many U.S. highway miles need renewal on difficult ground under time and traffic constraints.
sections.body: When difficult ground is encountered, the alternatives are (1) bypassing it by relocation or a deep foundation, (2) removing and replacing the unsuitable soils, (3) designing the structure to accommodate it, or (4) modifying (improving) the existing soils in place or by removal, treatment and replacement (ASCE 1978; Mitchell 1981). Terms vary ('soil improvement', 'ground improvement', 'ground treatment', 'ground modification'); Charles (2002) calls the process ground treatment, its purpose ground improvement and its result ground modification. Herein ground modification is the alteration of site foundation conditions or project earth structures to provide better performance under design and/or operational loading conditions (USACE 1999). Its primary functions: increase shear strength and bearing resistance; increase density; decrease permeability; control deformations (settlement, heave, distortions); increase drainage; accelerate consolidation; decrease imposed loads; provide lateral stability; increase resistance to liquefaction; transfer embankment loads to more competent subsurface layers. The U.S. has over four million miles of highways (over 164,000 on the National Highway System); the ASCE 2013 Report Card found 32% of major roads in poor or mediocre condition, costing motorists $67 billion a year. Much renewal is on difficult ground, under time constraints, with minimal traffic disruption, long-lived results and protection of adjacent facilities, so selecting a geoconstruction technology is complex. (pp. 1-1 to 1-2)
key_points: Four alternatives: bypass, remove and replace, design for, or modify the poor ground
Ground modification: altering site foundation conditions or earth structures for better performance (USACE 1999)
Ten primary functions, from increasing strength and density to transferring embankment loads

sections.title: Historical Overview
sections.summary: The basic soil improvement concepts are ancient (ASCE 1978); machines and soil mechanics made modern methods possible. Many methods came from Europe and the Far East, led by contractors, so practice often preceded research. FHWA Demonstration Project 116 found benefits in five areas, and ground modification is now routinely considered.
sections.body: The ASCE Committee on Placement and Improvement of Soils (1978) noted that the basic concepts of soil improvement (densification, cementation, reinforcement, drainage, drying, heating) were developed hundreds or thousands of years ago. Industrial Revolution machines greatly improved construction; drainage methods for roads (crowned grades, clean free-draining aggregate) followed; 20th-century soil mechanics and equipment led to densification, soil mixing, grouting and reinforcing methods. Many techniques originated in Europe and the Far East, often contractor-led, experience-based and sometimes proprietary; FHWA (DiMillio 1999) noted commercial and technological innovations have almost always preceded research and engineering guidelines. Demonstration Project No. 116, Ground Improvement Methods (Elias et al. 1999), found benefits in five areas: less costly foundation systems, reduced right-of-way acquisitions, less environmental disturbance, reduced construction time, and improved traffic control through work zones. Ground modification is now routinely considered where poor or unstable soils occur, especially suspect or uncontrolled fills; to the designer it modifies an engineering property or transfers load to competent layers, to the contractor it may cut time and cost. (pp. 1-2 to 1-3)
key_points: Basic soil improvement concepts are centuries old (ASCE 1978)
Contractor innovation usually preceded research and guidelines (DiMillio 1999)
Demonstration Project 116: five benefit areas, from cheaper foundations to traffic control

sections.title: Focus and Scope
sections.summary: The manual introduces ground modification methods to design generalists, specialists, construction and contracting staff. Chapter 1 covers functions, categories, risks, contracting, costs, GeoTechTools and a 12-step selection process; the category chapters follow a common outline. Table 1-1 lists the nine technical categories and their technologies.
sections.body: Over the last forty years new technologies have been developed for marginal sites. The manual introduces ground modification methods and applications to design generalists (planners, roadway designers, consultant reviewers), design specialists (geotechnical, structural, pavement), construction engineers and specification and contracting specialists. Chapter 1 gives the description, history, functions and categories of ground modification, its role in project risks and constraints, contracting mechanisms, typical unit costs, the GeoTechTools website (geotechtools.org) for initial screening, and a 12-step process leading to a preferred technology. Each category chapter gives a broad introduction, typical applications and technology summaries covering description, advantages and limitations, applicability, complementary technologies, construction methods and materials, photographs, design guidance, quality assurance, costs, specifications and references, with selected transportation case histories. Table 1-1: ch 2 Vertical Drains and Accelerated Consolidation (PVDs with and without fill preloading); ch 3 Lightweight Fills (granular fills: wood fiber, blast furnace slag, fly ash, boiler slag, expanded shale, clay and slate, shredded tires; compressive strength fills: geofoam, foamed concrete); ch 4 Deep Compaction (deep dynamic compaction, vibro-compaction); ch 5 Aggregate Columns (stone columns, rammed aggregate piers); ch 6 Column Supported Embankments (CSE, reinforced soil load transfer platform, non-compressible and compressible columns); ch 7 Soil Mixing (deep mixing, mass mixing); ch 8 Grouting (chemical (permeation), compaction, bulk void filling, slabjacking, jet, rock fissure); ch 9 Pavement Support Stabilization (mechanical, chemical, moisture control); ch 10 Reinforced Soil Structures (reinforced embankments, walls, slopes, soil nailing). (pp. 1-4 to 1-5)
key_points: Audience: design generalists and specialists, construction, specification and contracting staff
Chapter 1 ends in a 12-step process to select a preferred technology

sections.title: Typical Functions and Typical Applications
sections.summary: Ground modification has been categorized by Mitchell (1981), Munfakh and Wyllie (2000, eight categories) and ISSMGE TC 211 (five categories); this manual categorizes by the functions of Section 1.1. Applications: bridge support, embankments, embankment widening, pavement support and construction working platforms.
sections.body: Methods can be categorized many ways. Mitchell (1981): compaction (in-situ deep densification of cohesionless soils); consolidation by preloading and/or vertical drains and electro-osmosis; grouting; stabilization by admixtures and ion exchange; thermal stabilization; reinforcement. Munfakh and Wyllie (2000): densification, consolidation, weight reduction, reinforcement, chemical treatment, thermal stabilization, electrotreatment and biotechnical stabilization. ISSMGE TC 211 (formerly TC17): improvement without admixtures in non-cohesive soils; without admixtures in cohesive soils; with admixtures or inclusions; with grouting type admixtures; earth reinforcement (Chu et al. 2009). Herein technologies are categorized by the functions of Section 1.1 (detailed in 2.1.1). Transportation applications are bridge support, embankments, embankment widening, pavement support and construction working platforms (2.1.2). (p. 1-6)
key_points: Categorizations: Mitchell (1981), Munfakh and Wyllie (2000), ISSMGE TC 211
This manual categorizes technologies by function (Section 1.1)
Applications: bridge support, embankments, widening, pavement support, working platforms
sections.applicability: Matching ground modification technologies to project soil conditions and functional requirements.

sections.title: Functions
sections.summary: Heading for the ten functions of ground modification, each defined in 2.1.1.1 to 2.1.1.10.
sections.body: Heading for the functions of ground modification introduced in Section 1.1; each of the ten is defined in the subsections that follow (2.1.1.1 to 2.1.1.10). (p. 1-6)
sections.applicability: The functions ground modification can serve.

sections.title: Increase Shear Strength and Bearing Resistance
sections.summary: Raising soil strength raises bearing resistance for foundations and embankments, by densifying loose cohesionless soils, consolidating soft clays, or adding cementing agents.
sections.body: Here ground modification increases the soil's strength, which in turn increases bearing resistance for foundations and embankments. This can be done by densifying loose cohesionless soils, consolidating soft clay soils, or adding cementing agents to the soil. (p. 1-6)
key_points: Densify loose cohesionless soils, consolidate soft clays, or add cementing agents
sections.applicability: Identifying the ground modification function a project needs.

sections.title: Increase density
sections.summary: Densifying loose sands by vibratory or dynamic energy raises strength, bearing resistance and liquefaction resistance; in cohesive soils density rises by consolidation, which reduces settlement under later loads.
sections.body: This function generally applies to densifying loose sands by technologies that add energy through vibration or a dynamic process, changing loose sand into a denser state with increased strength, bearing resistance and resistance to liquefaction. In cohesive soils density is increased by consolidation, which removes water from the voids and so reduces the settlement that occurs when loads are applied. (pp. 1-6 to 1-7)
key_points: Loose sands: vibratory or dynamic energy
Cohesive soils: consolidation removes pore water
sections.applicability: Identifying the ground modification function a project needs.

sections.title: Decrease Permeability
sections.summary: Reducing water flow through soil by densifying it or adding grouts or binders that make it relatively impermeable or fill fissures.
sections.body: The function is to decrease the amount of water flowing through the soil, by increasing its density or by adding grouts or binders that make the soil relatively impermeable or fill fissures. (p. 1-7)
key_points: Densify, or add grouts or binders
sections.applicability: Identifying the ground modification function a project needs.

sections.title: Control Deformation
sections.summary: Reducing total settlement, heave and differential distortion by densifying, consolidating or binding soils, by columns transferring load to competent materials, or by binders against expansive heave.
sections.body: Controlling deformation includes reducing total settlement, heave, and distortion caused by differential settlement. Methods densify or consolidate the foundation soils, or strengthen them with grouts or binders; columns can transfer loads to more competent materials; expansive soil heave can be treated with binders that mitigate the effects of water. (p. 1-7)
key_points: Densify, consolidate or bind soils, or use columns to competent layers
Binders can treat expansive soil heave
sections.applicability: Identifying the ground modification function a project needs.

sections.title: Increase Drainage
sections.summary: Removing water from foundation soils, subgrades and base and subbase courses improves almost all soils' strength and stiffness, and can reduce liquefaction susceptibility of cohesionless materials.
sections.body: Increasing drainage allows more efficient removal of water from foundation soils, subgrades, and base and subbase courses. Almost all soils improve in strength and stiffness with reduced water. Increased drainage can also reduce liquefaction susceptibility of cohesionless materials. (p. 1-7)
key_points: Less water improves strength and stiffness of almost all soils
Drainage can also reduce liquefaction susceptibility
sections.applicability: Identifying the ground modification function a project needs.

sections.title: Accelerate Consolidation
sections.summary: Shortening the drainage path in cohesive soils, with embankment or fill preloading, by prefabricated vertical drains or other columns that give water an easier flow path.
sections.body: Accelerating consolidation reduces the time for foundation settlement to occur. It is done by reducing the drainage path length in cohesive soils, combined with embankment loading or fill preloading, using prefabricated vertical drains or other columns that give water an easier flow path. (p. 1-7)
key_points: Shorter drainage path plus embankment or fill preloading (PVDs or other columns)
sections.applicability: Identifying the ground modification function a project needs.

sections.title: Decrease Imposed Loads
sections.summary: Lighter weight fill materials reduce loads on weak soils, reducing settlement and stability problems.
sections.body: Decreasing imposed loads by using lighter weight fill materials reduces loads on weak soils, reducing settlement and stability issues. (p. 1-7)
key_points: Lightweight fills reduce settlement and stability problems
sections.applicability: Identifying the ground modification function a project needs.

sections.title: Provide Lateral Stability
sections.summary: Earth retaining systems give lateral support and stability to site soils for grade changes in cut and fill, vertical or sloping.
sections.body: Changes in grade can be accomplished with a number of earth retaining systems that provide lateral support and stability to site soils, in both cut and fill situations, for both vertical and sloping cases. (p. 1-8)
key_points: Earth retaining systems in cut or fill, vertical or sloping
sections.applicability: Identifying the ground modification function a project needs.

sections.title: Increase Resistance to Liquefaction
sections.summary: Densifying cohesionless soils by vibratory or dynamic methods, adding grouts and binders, increasing drainage, or isolating the potentially liquefiable soils.
sections.body: Resistance of cohesionless soils to liquefaction can be increased by densifying them by vibratory or dynamic methods. Other means are adding grouts and binders to the soil matrix, increasing drainage, and isolating the potentially liquefiable soils. (p. 1-8)
key_points: Densification, grouts or binders, drainage, or isolation
sections.applicability: Identifying the ground modification function a project needs.

sections.title: Transfer Vertical Loads to More Competent Soil or Rock Layers
sections.summary: Columns carry vertical loads, typically embankments or fill retaining structures, through loose or weak soils to competent layers, controlling settlement (especially differential) and stability.
sections.body: Vertical loads, typically embankments or fill retaining structures, are transferred through loose or weak soils by columns to more competent layers. This helps control settlement, particularly differential settlement, and the stability of the highway feature on unstable soils. (p. 1-8)
key_points: Columns carry embankment loads through weak soils
Controls differential settlement and stability
sections.applicability: Identifying the ground modification function a project needs.

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: Heading for the highway and transportation applications of ground modification, each discussed in 2.1.2.1 to 2.1.2.5.
sections.body: Ground modification and geoconstruction technologies can be used in a number of highway and transportation infrastructure applications; the common ones are discussed in 2.1.2.1 to 2.1.2.5. (p. 1-8)
sections.applicability: Transportation applications of ground modification.

sections.title: Structure Support
sections.summary: Bridges at water crossings often sit on interlayered, non-uniform alluvium; ground modification can improve the site so cheaper shallow or intermediate foundations replace deep foundations; retaining structures can serve as abutments and approach embankments.
sections.body: Bridges cross water and provide grade separations. At water crossings the bridge is often in an alluvial environment with soft clays to loose and dense sands, often interlayered and non-uniform. Deep foundations often support abutments and piers, but ground modification can improve site conditions so that less expensive shallow or intermediate foundations can be used. Retaining structures can also serve as abutments and approach embankments. (p. 1-8)
key_points: Alluvial bridge sites are often interlayered and non-uniform
Ground modification can allow shallow or intermediate foundations instead of deep ones
sections.applicability: Transportation applications of ground modification.

sections.title: Embankments
sections.summary: Embankments change grade and approach bridges, often across unstable soils; ground modification reduces settlement and stability problems without excavating and disposing of the unsuitable soil.
sections.body: Embankments support highways, change grade along an alignment and serve as bridge approaches. They are often built across unstable soils; ground modification can improve the foundation soils to reduce settlement and stability issues while avoiding excavation and disposal of the unsuitable soil. (pp. 1-8 to 1-9)
key_points: Improves unstable foundations without excavation and disposal
sections.applicability: Transportation applications of ground modification.

sections.title: Embankment Widening
sections.summary: Adding lanes on compressible soils risks differential settlement between old and new embankment and global instability; lightweight fills, column supported embankments and methods raising bearing resistance help.
sections.body: Adding lanes to roads on compressible, unstable soils by adding embankment can cause differential settlement between existing and new embankments, global instability, etc. Ground modification can stabilize the soils using lightweight fill materials, column supported embankments, and methods that increase the bearing resistance of the underlying soils. (p. 1-9)
key_points: Risk: differential settlement between existing and new embankment
Lightweight fills, column supported embankments, bearing improvement
sections.applicability: Transportation applications of ground modification.

sections.title: Pavement Support
sections.summary: Poor subgrades need thick structural sections and may not carry construction equipment; subgrade and base layers can be improved mechanically, chemically, by alternative or recycled materials, and by drainage.
sections.body: The pavement section rests on subgrade soil that may be poor, requiring very thick structural sections, and may not even support construction equipment. Support can be increased by stabilizing the subgrade and using alternative or recycled materials; subgrade and base layers can be improved mechanically and chemically, and by drainage to reduce the adverse effects of water. (p. 1-9)
key_points: Mechanical, chemical and drainage improvement of subgrade and base
sections.applicability: Transportation applications of ground modification.

sections.title: Construction Working Platform
sections.summary: Working platforms are almost always needed to carry ground modification equipment on poor soils, and for temporary roads and storage; they are supported like pavements but are temporary.
sections.body: Construction platforms are almost always needed to support ground modification equipment on the poor soils being stabilized, and often for temporary roadways and equipment and material storage. Their means of support is similar to pavement support but considered temporary. (p. 1-9)
key_points: Almost always needed for ground modification equipment on poor soils
Temporary pavement-like support
sections.applicability: Transportation applications of ground modification.

sections.title: Applicability Limits
sections.summary: Every technology has applicability limits (soil type, treatment depth, etc.); Table 1-2 summarizes general applicability by category, e.g., DDC for loose pervious soils with fines under 15%, vibro-compaction for clean sands with under 15% silt and/or 2% clay, aggregate columns for clays, silts, loose silty sands and uncompacted fill.
sections.body: All ground modification technologies have limits on applicability, such as soil type and depth of treatment. Table 1-2 summarizes general applicability by category; advantages and disadvantages are in the category chapters. Table 1-2: PVDs - compressible clays, saturated low strength clays; lightweight fills (compressive strength and granular) - broad applicability, no geologic or geometric limitations; deep dynamic compaction - loose pervious and semi-pervious soils with fines contents less than 15%, materials with large voids, spoils and waste areas; vibro-compaction - cohesionless soils, clean sands with less than 15% silts and/or less than 2% clay; stone columns and rammed aggregate piers - clays, silts, loose silty sands, uncompacted fill; column supported embankments and load transfer platforms - soft compressible clay, peats and organic soils where settlement and global stability are concerns; non-compressible columns - all soil types, in particular weak soils that cannot support surface loads; compressible columns - all soil types except very soft soils (low undrained shear strength); deep mixing - a large range of soils that can be stabilized with cement, lime, slag or other binders; mass mixing - peat, soft clay, dredged soil, soft silt, sludges, contaminated soils; chemical grouting - wide range including weakly cemented rock-fill; compaction grouting - cohesionless granular, collapsible and unsaturated fine grained soils, voids in sinkholes or mine shafts, arresting settlement and lifting foundations; jet grouting - wide range of soils and groundwater conditions; rock fissure grouting - structural stability and groundwater control; bulk void filling and slabjacking - all soils where voids develop under pavements; mechanical stabilization - weak subgrades, loose sands, thin aggregate layers on subgrades with CBR < 8; chemical stabilization - portland cement and lime for high plasticity clays, fly ash for soils with little or no plastic fines, asphalt for silty, sandy and granular soils, cement kiln dust for expansive soils; moisture control - all soils; reinforced embankments - soft foundations with no depth limit; reinforced soil walls - fill embankments, steep terrain, unstable ground, poor foundations; reinforced soil slopes - any firm foundation; soil nail walls - dense granular soils with apparent cohesion, weathered rock, stiff fine-grained soils, engineered fill, residual soils, glacial till. (pp. 1-9 to 1-11)
key_points: Limits are by soil type, treatment depth and similar
DDC: loose pervious soils with fines < 15%; vibro-compaction: clean sands, < 15% silt and/or < 2% clay
Mechanical pavement stabilization: subgrades with CBR < 8
Table 1-2: general applicability of each technology
sections.applicability: Screening criteria for determining whether a ground modification technology is feasible for a given site.

sections.title: Feasibility Evaluations
sections.summary: Feasibility depends on the function and method; evaluate technical issues, delivery methods, performance criteria and QA, and non-technical issues, in seven steps from identifying project conditions needing ground modification to considering alternatives.
sections.body: Feasibility of a method for a project depends on the function(s) of the modification and the method(s) selected. The evaluation identifies and evaluates technical issues, project development and delivery methods, performance criteria and quality assurance, and non-technical issues. Generalized process: 1 identify project conditions that could require ground modification or geoconstruction: (a) poor ground conditions (soft or loose foundation soils causing long-term vertical and/or lateral deformation or instability), (b) constraints requiring retaining walls or steep slopes, (c) pavement foundations requiring improvement, (d) need for a working platform or access road; 2 identify or establish performance requirements; 3 identify time, space or environmental constraints; 4 assess site conditions; 5 assess project constraints; 6 identify limitations on ground modification; 7 consider alternatives. (pp. 1-11 to 1-12)
key_points: Seven-step feasibility evaluation
Triggers: poor ground, walls or steep slopes, pavement foundations, working platforms
sections.applicability: Preliminary screening and feasibility assessment for ground modification projects.

sections.title: Project Constraints
sections.summary: Project constraints: schedule, phasing, budget, right-of-way, geometry, utilities, traffic, weather and environment; schedule acceleration makes construction speed a key selection factor.
sections.body: Project constraints are generally the schedule and time, phasing, budget and cost, project conditions (right-of-way limits, geometry, scale, utilities and sequence), traffic flow, interruption and congestion, weather, and environmental factors. Schedule acceleration matters on almost all projects, so speed of ground modification construction is often a key selection factor. (p. 1-12)
key_points: Speed of construction is often a key selection factor
sections.applicability: Screening ground modification against project constraints.

sections.title: Geotechnical Performance Criteria/Indicators
sections.summary: Performance criteria are the facility's operational criteria: stability, allowable total or differential settlement, settlement rate, seepage, durability and maintenance; they set the required improvement in strength, density, modulus, compressibility and hydraulic conductivity.
sections.body: Performance requirements, the operational criteria for the facility, are typically geotechnical: stability requirements, allowable long-term deformations (total or differential settlement), rate of settlement, seepage (quantity and flow rate), and durability (service life) and maintenance. They set the level of improvement required in soil properties such as strength, density, modulus, compressibility and hydraulic conductivity. (pp. 1-12 to 1-13)
key_points: Criteria: stability, settlement and its rate, seepage, durability
They set the required soil property improvement
sections.applicability: Setting performance criteria for ground modification.

sections.title: Environmental and Space Considerations
sections.summary: Environmental constraints (spoil and waste disposal, erosion, water pollution, vibration, noise, dust) and space constraints (access, room for equipment, overhead clearance, adjacent structures and utilities) must be assessed.
sections.body: Environmental constraints may include disposal of spoils from the technology and of waste found on site, erosion protection, protection of surface and ground waters from pollution, and construction vibrations, noise and dust. Space constraints are site accessibility, sufficient area for equipment to operate safely, overhead clearance, and adjacent structures and utilities. (p. 1-13)
key_points: Environmental: spoils, waste, erosion, pollution, vibration, noise, dust
Space: access, working room, headroom, adjacent structures and utilities
sections.applicability: Screening ground modification against site environment and space.

sections.title: Site Conditions
sections.summary: Site conditions mean first the subsurface: at minimum the type, depth and extent of needed treatment and the groundwater table; preferably shear strength, compressibility and organic content; also obstructions, water bearing sands, organic layers, stiff crusts and local materials.
sections.body: Site conditions mean first and foremost the subsurface conditions, assessed in detail that varies with the project and the method. The soils affecting performance must be identified and their properties established for preliminary design. At minimum the type, depth and extent of needed treatment and the groundwater table must be determined; for poor ground a preliminary assessment of shear strength, compressibility and organic content is valuable. Obstructions (cobbles, boulders, construction debris), water bearing sands, organic layers and very stiff surface deposits affect selection, as does availability of sand, gravel and water. (p. 1-13)
key_points: Minimum: type, depth and extent of treatment, groundwater table
Obstructions, organic layers and stiff crusts affect selection
sections.applicability: Assessing site conditions for ground modification.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.summary: General limitations (knowledge, policies, design procedures, QA, performance uncertainty, equipment and staff), site limitations, the ASD basis of most methods (not LRFD-calibrated), proprietary or black box designs, and technology limits such as headroom, depth and time.
sections.body: Limitations may be general, site-related or technology dependent. General: lack of knowledge, of organizational structure and policies encouraging innovation, of simple reliable design procedures and effective QA; undefined parameters or performance criteria; long-term performance uncertainty; availability of equipment, experienced staff and materials. These can be overcome by promotion, collaboration, education, agency technology champions, documented case histories and demonstration projects. Site: lack of characterization, environmental constraints, obstructions above and below ground, nearby development, unusual loads and vibrations. Most techniques have traditionally been designed by allowable stress design rather than LRFD and have not been calibrated in the LRFD conversion (unlike structural foundations and MSE and soil nail walls); many do not lend themselves to LRFD; some are proprietary or have black box designs. Each technology also has limits such as headroom, depth, design and QA requirements, and time to construct and become effective. (pp. 1-13 to 1-14)
key_points: Most ground modification methods are ASD-based, not LRFD-calibrated
Some methods are proprietary or have black box design
Technology limits: headroom, depth, QA, time to become effective
sections.applicability: Recognizing limits on using ground modification.

sections.title: Alternative Solutions
sections.summary: Alternatives should always be considered: relocation, deep foundations, removal and replacement, designing for the poor ground, or a structural solution such as a bridge.
sections.body: Ground modification is not the only feasible way to address poor ground, and alternatives should always be considered: bypassing it by relocation or deep foundations, removing and replacing the unsuitable soils, designing the structure to accommodate the poor ground, or a structural solution such as a bridge. (p. 1-14)
key_points: Always consider bypass, replacement, design for the ground, or a bridge
sections.applicability: Weighing alternatives to ground modification.

sections.title: Technology Classification and Elements
sections.summary: Part 3.0 (pp. 1-15 to 1-19): classification of the manual's technologies by function (Table 1-3) and the four elements of construction they serve (Figure 1-1).
sections.body: Heading of part 3.0, Technology Classification and Elements; it has no text of its own before 3.1. Its sections classify technologies by function (3.1) and describe the elements of construction (3.2). (p. 1-15)
sections.applicability: Systematic classification framework for organizing and selecting ground modification technologies.

sections.title: Classification by Function
sections.summary: Table 1-3 classifies the manual's technologies by the functions of 1.1 and 2.1.1, with much overlap. GeoTechTools instead lists technologies under eleven geotechnical solutions, from earthwork construction to sustainability.
sections.body: Technologies are classified by the functions of Sections 1.1 and 2.1.1 in Table 1-3, with considerable overlap as many fit several functions. Table 1-3 rows (technologies; comment): increase shear strength and bearing resistance (vibro-compaction, dynamic compaction, compaction grouting, mixing methods, PVDs, stone columns, rammed aggregate piers, chemical and mechanical stabilization; some work in all soils, others only cohesive or cohesionless); increase density (vibro-compaction, dynamic compaction, blasting compaction, compaction grouting, mixing methods, PVDs); decrease permeability (bulk-infill, chemical and jet grouting, deep mixing; grouting type depends on soils, depths, geology and design); control deformations (column supported embankments, reinforced load transfer platforms, non-compressible columns, mixing, vibro and dynamic compaction, stone columns, rammed aggregate piers, chemical and mechanical stabilization, encapsulation; bypass or isolate or improve soft ground); increase drainage (PVDs, aggregate columns, geotextile encased columns, electro-osmosis, geosynthetics in pavement drainage); accelerate consolidation (PVDs, aggregate columns, geotextile encased columns; shorter flow path); decrease imposed loads (granular and compressive strength lightweight fills; densities 1 to 90 pcf, granular fills subject to local availability); provide lateral stability (MSE walls, reinforced soil slopes, soil nailing); increase resistance to liquefaction (aggregate columns, deep dynamic compaction, deep mixing, jet grouting, vibro-compaction; aggregate columns also drain); transfer embankment loads (column supported embankments, load transfer platforms, non-compressible and compressible columns). GeoTechTools lists technologies under earthwork construction, soft ground drainage and consolidation, densification of cohesionless soils, vertical support elements, embankments over soft soils, lateral earth support, cutoff walls, liquefaction mitigation, increased pavement performance, void filling and sustainability. (pp. 1-15 to 1-16)
key_points: Table 1-3: technologies classified by function, with much overlap
Lightweight fill densities range from 1 to 90 pcf
GeoTechTools classifies by eleven geotechnical solutions
sections.applicability: Detailed functional classification for identifying technologies that address specific engineering needs.

sections.title: Elements of Construction
sections.summary: Four elements of construction (Figure 1-1): construction over unstable soils (below-grade improvement), construction over stable or stabilized soils (above-grade embankment, retention and slopes), geotechnical pavement components, and working platforms (generally temporary).
sections.body: Difficult ground is typically soft or loose foundation soil that would settle excessively or become unstable under load. The technologies apply to four elements of construction, shown in Figure 1-1 and often used with structures such as bridges. Construction over Unstable Soils: supporting embankments and widening on weak or loose foundations, typically below-grade improvement (some at-grade), for abutment support, approach embankments, widening and structural elements. Construction over Stable or Stabilized Soils: above-grade embankment and widening methods (fill placement and compaction, reduced embankment width or volume, fill earth retention, slope stabilization) for abutment retaining systems and reduced right-of-way. Geotechnical Pavement Components: improving subgrade, base and subbase by fill placement, stabilization, grouting and reinforcement, including recycling and reuse. Working Platforms: on stable or unstable subgrades by fill placement, stabilization and reinforcement; also applicable to the first and third elements; generally temporary. (pp. 1-17 to 1-19)
key_points: Figure 1-1: four elements of construction
Over unstable soils (below-grade) vs over stable or stabilized soils (above-grade)
Pavement components and working platforms (generally temporary)
sections.applicability: Understanding how construction element type influences design methodology selection.

sections.title: Constraints and Risk Management
sections.summary: Constraints restrict activities and can pose risks to project delivery and performance; risks can be managed by a risk management process, and ground modification can mitigate some risks and work within constraints.
sections.body: Constraints are limitations or restrictions on activities that can affect delivery and performance; often project specific, they can pose risks to completion and performance, which can be identified and managed through a risk management process. Ground modification can mitigate some project risks and can be selected to work within a set of constraints. Sections 4.1 to 4.3 cover types of constraints, types of risks and the risk management process. (p. 1-20)
key_points: Constraints can pose risks; a risk management process manages them
Ground modification can mitigate some risks within the project constraints
sections.applicability: Risk identification and management framework for ground modification projects.

sections.title: Types of Constraints
sections.summary: Project constraints may be economic, legal, environmental, social, management, time or technical; herein they are grouped as general and geotechnical. Early identification and clear definition are the key to mitigation.
sections.body: Constraints are often driven by factors external to the owner and vary by project, in economic, legal, environmental, social, management, time and technical areas. With the emphasis on ground modification they are defined in two categories, general and geotechnical. The key to constraint mitigation is early identification and clear definition. (p. 1-20)
key_points: Two categories: general and geotechnical
Identify and define constraints early
sections.applicability: Identifying project constraints affecting ground modification.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: General constraints are non-geotechnical: schedule, budget, right-of-way, geometry, utilities, traffic, weather, environment, agency staff and organization, contracting, public perception and liability; identify them early.
sections.body: General constraints are all items not explicitly connected with the geotechnical aspects: schedule and time; budget and cost; right-of-way limits, geometry, scale, utilities and sequence; traffic flow and interruption; weather; environmental; agency personnel, organization and structure; project management philosophy; contracting processes; public perceptions; and liability. Some act throughout, others at certain phases. Identify them as early as possible for a proactive approach. Time, for example, covers planning, design, procurement and construction, and a delay in one phase may affect the whole schedule. (p. 1-20)
key_points: Non-geotechnical constraints, from schedule to liability
A delay in one phase may affect the whole project
sections.applicability: Identifying general project constraints.

sections.title: Geotechnical
sections.summary: Geotechnical constraints: subsurface conditions (archaeology, contaminated groundwater, obstructions, utilities), proprietary products, experience, allowable movements, stability, noise and vibration, time to take effect, spoils, environmental impact, contractor and equipment availability, constructability.
sections.body: Geotechnical constraints are specific to the geotechnical aspects and the candidate technologies: subsurface conditions including archaeological remains, contaminated groundwater, obstructions and buried utilities; proprietary products and processes; knowledge and experience with specific technologies; allowable vertical and lateral movements; stability requirements; construction noise and vibration; time for the modification to become effective; spoils development, volume and disposal; environmental impacts; availability of qualified contractors, personnel, materials and specialty equipment; and constructability. (pp. 1-20 to 1-21)
key_points: Includes time for the modification to become effective
Includes spoils, vibration, proprietary systems, contractor availability
sections.applicability: Identifying geotechnical project constraints.

sections.title: Types of Risks
sections.summary: Risk is probability times consequence (Baecher and Christian 2003); geotechnical risks include instability, deformation, liquefaction, unforeseen conditions and inadequate investigation, design or construction. Delivery methods shift risks without removing them; Table 1-4 compares D-B-B and D-B risk profiles (Gransberg and Loulakis 2012).
sections.body: In engineering, risk is the product of the probability of an event and its consequences (Baecher and Christian 2003); a geotechnical risk is an adverse geotechnical outcome affecting the project, from delay to redesign of a component. A key risk is failing to identify problems and design for them. Possible risks: slope instability; vertical and lateral deformations; bearing capacity; liquefaction; subsidence; groundwater levels and fluctuations; chemically reactive ground; contamination; unforeseen ground conditions (differing site conditions); problem soils (expansive, collapsible, organic/peat, dispersive, fills, landfills); inadequate investigation; inadequate design; poor construction or monitoring; also material characterization, models, service conditions, loads and resistance. Contract disputes in highway work are often geotechnical. Risks can be accepted, managed and mitigated (Chapman 2012); sound practice such as hazard recognition reduces them. Under Design-Bid-Build, Design-Build, P3 and CMGC the risks remain but shift among participants. A TRB synthesis (Gransberg and Loulakis 2012) compared geotechnical scope, cost and schedule risk between D-B-B and D-B (Table 1-4); design errors and omissions, latent design defects and market fluctuation during design move from the owner in D-B-B to the design-builder in D-B. (pp. 1-21 to 1-24)
key_points: Risk = probability x consequence (Baecher and Christian 2003)
A key risk is failing to identify problems and design for them
Delivery methods shift geotechnical risks; they do not remove them
Table 1-4: D-B-B vs D-B scope, cost and schedule risk profiles

sections.title: Risk Management Process
sections.summary: Risk management systematically identifies, analyzes, evaluates, treats and monitors risk, with a risk register and response and tracking plans. The SHRP2 R09 process (Golder Associates 2011, Figure 1-2) loops through structuring, risk identification, assessment, analysis, management planning and implementation.
sections.body: Risk management is 'the systematic application of management policies, procedures and practices to the activities of communicating, consulting, establishing the context, and identifying, analyzing, evaluating, treating, monitoring and reviewing risk.' It sets the context, objectives and criteria; risks are identified, analyzed, assessed and prioritized in a risk register; response plans and a tracking plan follow, at project, program or enterprise level, with communication at every step. Ground modification decisions have often been reactive; risk management allows proactive use. The SHRP2 R09 study (Golder Associates Inc. 2011) aims to optimize project performance efficiently, defensibly and adequately. Its six-step loop (Figure 1-2): 1 Structuring (base project scope, strategy, conditions); 2 Risk Identification (risks and opportunities, start a non-overlapping risk register); 3 Risk Assessment (relative severity, prioritization, updated as the project develops); 4 Risk Analysis (quantitative, with uncertainty, probability distributions and sensitivity, for complex projects); 5 Risk Management Planning (proactive responses, reviewed as risks change); 6 Risk Management Implementation (implement and monitor the plan, with periodic review). (pp. 1-24 to 1-26)
key_points: Risk register, response plans and tracking plan
Figure 1-2: SHRP2 R09 six-step iterative process (Golder Associates 2011)
Steps: structuring, identification, assessment, analysis, planning, implementation
figures: Figure 1-2: SHRP 2 R09 iterative risk management process.
