sections.title: Contracting Alternatives, Specifications, and Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Contracting methods affect how constraints are found and risks managed; part 5.0 covers contracting mechanisms, specifications, quality assurance, and construction control and instrumentation monitoring.
sections.body: Project planning is concerned with understanding constraints and identifying risks, which are always present; their discernment and management can be affected by the contracting method. Sections 5.1 to 5.5 discuss contract mechanisms, specifications, quality assurance, and instrumentation monitoring and construction control. (p. 1-27)
key_points: Contracting methods affect how constraints and risks are handled
sections.applicability: Contract structure and quality assurance framework for ground modification projects.

sections.title: Contracting Mechanisms Used in Project Delivery
sections.summary: Project delivery spans planning to close-out; contracting assigns design and construction roles. Figure 1-3 shows the Federal Lands Highway development process. Besides design-bid-build: design-build (one contract), P3 (private financing and operation) and CMGC (contractor input during design, then negotiated construction); risks shift, not vanish.
sections.body: Project delivery is the whole process from planning and programming to construction close-out; contracting refers to roles for design and construction. Agencies estimate and control costs, meet environmental and Federal requirements, obtain financing and manage the parties. State processes generally include planning and programming, conceptual studies, environmental stewardship, right-of-way, preliminary design, final design and PS&E, and construction. Figure 1-3 (Federal Lands Highway PDDM, FHWA 2011): needs studies and requests lead to a long-range plan and programming, project scoping (data, standards, preliminary engineering), preliminary design (environmental work in scoping or preliminary design), final design and PS&E, then construction. Traditionally design-bid-build (lowest responsible bidder); newer methods are Design-Build (one design-build team under a single, generally fixed-fee contract), Public-Private-Partnerships (private participation in delivery and financing, often operation and tolls for a period, with substantial private risk) and CMGC (a contractor advises during design on risks, costs and schedule, then the construction price is negotiated; often used to accelerate delivery). As in Section 4.2, these methods shift risks among the parties rather than eliminate them. (pp. 1-27 to 1-29)
key_points: Project delivery spans planning to close-out; contracting assigns roles
Figure 1-3: Federal Lands Highway project development work process
D-B-B, D-B, P3 and CMGC shift risk rather than remove it
figures: Figure 1-3: Federal Lands Highway project development work process.
sections.applicability: Contracting methods for delivering ground modification projects.

sections.title: Specification Development
sections.summary: Specifications, part of the contract documents, give bidders and the contractor the owner's directions, procedures and material and equipment requirements; DOTs often lack them for ground modification, so the category chapters and GeoTechTools guide specifications help develop them.
sections.body: Specifications are the written instructions describing the work, part of the contract documents with drawings, bid documents, agreement forms and modifications. They communicate the owner's directions, procedures and material and equipment requirements before and after award and directly affect quality and cost (FHWA 2010; Scott et al. 2014). State DOTs often lack specifications or special provisions for ground modification, or have them only for methods they have used, so they often must be developed for a project. The category chapters give guidance, and GeoTechTools (Section 7) gives guide specifications, in many cases a preferred one, for each technology. (pp. 1-29 to 1-30)
key_points: DOTs often lack ground modification specifications
Guidance in the category chapters and GeoTechTools guide specifications
sections.applicability: Developing specifications for ground modification.

sections.title: Quality Assurance
sections.summary: QA is all planned actions giving confidence of satisfactory service (TRB 2002) and now includes contractor QC and agency acceptance. A QA program needs all six core elements: contractor QC, agency acceptance, independent assurance, dispute resolution, laboratory accreditation, personnel qualification; it is the same for D-B-B and D-B.
sections.body: TRB Circular E-C037 (TRB 2002) defines Quality Assurance as 'all those planned and systematic actions necessary to provide confidence that a product or facility will perform satisfactorily in service', spanning planning to maintenance. QC/QA once meant contractor QC and owner QA; QA is now the umbrella term covering the contractor's QC and the agency's acceptance. AASHTO (2006), FHWA (2008) and 23 CFR 637 define six core elements: 1 contractor quality control; 2 agency acceptance; 3 agency independent assurance; 4 dispute resolution; 5 laboratory accreditation and qualification; 6 personnel qualification/certification. All six are needed; a program missing any is not 'substantially compliant'. The contractor performs all QC to ensure the specified quality; acceptance is the agency's certification, sampling, testing and inspection to evaluate compliance and value, including monitoring the contractor's QC. The QA program is unaffected by D-B-B or D-B contracting. (pp. 1-30 to 1-31)
key_points: QA now covers contractor QC and agency acceptance
Six core elements, all required (AASHTO 2006, FHWA 2008, 23 CFR 637)
The QA program does not change with D-B-B or D-B
sections.applicability: Quality assurance programs for ground modification construction.

sections.title: Construction Control and Instrumentation Monitoring
sections.summary: Instrumentation and monitoring are routine in ground modification because foundation properties and their variation are hard to quantify; the main reason is managing risk (Marr 2013), with ten purposes listed. Table 1-5 lists sensors used to monitor geotechnical performance (Marr 2007b).
sections.body: Monitoring gives QA on methods and materials and reduces risks from variable in situ soil properties, which are hard to sample and quantify, so instrumentation is routine in ground modification. Field observations let the engineer design safely and efficiently and the contractor work safely and economically (Dunnicliff 1988); the primary reason is to help manage risk (Marr 2013). Monitoring verifies design during construction (staged construction, test sections) and performance afterward. Marr (2013) reasons: 1 show performance is safe and acceptable; 2 warn of impending failure; 3 reveal unknowns and aid the Observational Method; 4 evaluate the contractor's means and methods; 5 control construction or operations; 6 minimize damage to adjacent structures; 7 inform stakeholders; 8 satisfy regulators; 9 document performance for damage assessment; 10 improve performance and knowledge. Under performance specifications, instrumentation shows whether means and methods meet requirements, warns early, and can identify ineffective methods (Marr 2007a). Real-time monitoring is now cost-effective (Marr 2007b). Table 1-5: observation well, piezometer, earth pressure and contact pressure cells, load cell, settlement plate and gage, deformation monitoring point, flow meter and weir, crack meter, strain gage, tilt meter and inclinometer, borehole extensometer, geophone (1 to 400 Hz), accelerometer (1 to 4,000 Hz), temperature, barometer, automated total station and GPS (to about 0.05 inches), seismographs. (pp. 1-31 to 1-33)
key_points: Instrumentation is routine because ground properties vary and are hard to quantify
Primary purpose: manage risk (Marr 2013); ten reasons to monitor
Table 1-5: sensors for geotechnical monitoring (Marr 2007b)
tables: Table 1-5: Devices to Monitor Geotechnical Performance
sections.applicability: Instrumentation and construction control on ground modification projects.

sections.title: Considerations of QA in Ground Modification
sections.summary: QA in ground modification is complex: the contracting method affects who is responsible, so clear communication is needed, and QA methods range from simple to complex, which can affect whether a technology is selected.
sections.body: Selecting and applying QA methods for ground modification is complex. First, the contracting method affects responsibility for QA, so clear communication is needed to ensure appropriate methods and that each party conducts its responsibilities. Second, QA procedures range from simple to complex between technologies, and knowing them may affect the selection or desirability of a technology. (pp. 1-33 to 1-34)
key_points: Contracting method affects QA responsibility
QA complexity can affect technology selection
sections.applicability: Planning QA responsibilities for ground modification.

sections.title: Cost Analysis
sections.summary: Part 6.0 (pp. 1-35 to 1-37): cost components, factors influencing ground modification costs (Table 1-6 unit costs) and preliminary cost estimation.
sections.body: Heading of part 6.0, Cost Analysis; it has no text of its own before 6.1. Its sections cover general cost components (6.1), factors influencing cost with typical unit costs (6.2), and preliminary cost estimation (6.3). (p. 1-35)
sections.applicability: Cost estimation and economic comparison of ground modification technologies versus conventional alternatives.

sections.title: General Cost Components
sections.summary: A conceptual cost estimate identifies the components with the largest effect on cost; it needs a baseline cost for the technology, and costs have varied with the business cycle, contractor experience, equipment and competition; there is no average price for 'ground modification'.
sections.body: The section presents an approach for a ground modification cost estimate similar to a conceptual estimate: enough detail to identify the components with the largest effect on total cost, without specific bid quantities or bidders. It requires a baseline cost for the technology. Costs have varied over past decades mainly with the business cycle, specialty contractor experience, equipment advances and competition from conventional solutions. Given the variety of technologies there is no typical average price for 'ground modification'. (p. 1-35)
key_points: Conceptual estimate needs a baseline cost for the technology
No typical average price for 'ground modification'
sections.applicability: Estimating ground modification costs.

sections.title: Factors That Influence Ground Modification Costs
sections.summary: Primary costs are mobilization, materials, labor and equipment, plus QA (instrumentation, load tests); many factors affect them. Table 1-6 gives November 2016 unit costs, e.g., PVDs $0.50-$4/lft, DDC $10-$30/yd2, stone columns and rammed aggregate piers $15-$60/lft, jet grouting $250-$750/yd3; mobilization is extra.
sections.body: Primary cost items are mobilization, materials, labor and equipment, plus quality assurance including instrumentation and load tests. Factors include project type, application, technology, soil type, labor rates, utility conflicts, location, weather and competition. Costs are often rolled into prices per lineal or square foot of installed product. Table 1-6 (November 2016): PVDs $0.50-$4/lft; compressive strength lightweight fills $75-$150/yd3; granular lightweight fills $3-$15/yd3; deep dynamic compaction $10-$30/yd2; vibro-compaction $5-$9/lft; stone columns and rammed aggregate piers $15-$60/lft; column supported embankments $9/ft2 plus the column; non-compressible columns $30-$80/lft; compressible columns $20-$100/lft; deep mixing (dry) $60-$125/lft; mass mixing $15-$75/yd3; chemical grouting $20/ft + $0.65/qt; compaction grouting $75-$750/yd3; bulk void filling $50-$150/yd3; slabjacking $6.50-$9.30/ft2; jet grouting $250-$750/yd3; rock fissure grouting $25-$80/ft2; mechanical stabilization $1-$5/yd2; chemical stabilization $2-$5/yd2; moisture control $3-$12/lft; reinforced embankments $2-$12/yd2; MSE walls $30-$65/ft2; reinforced soil slopes $3-$25/ft2; soil nailing $20-$50/lft. Mobilization and demobilization is generally a lump sum from a few hundred dollars to more than $100,000; site investigation, QA testing and instrumentation are not in the unit prices. (pp. 1-35 to 1-37)
key_points: Primary costs: mobilization, materials, labor, equipment, plus QA
Table 1-6: comparative unit costs, November 2016
Mobilization: a few hundred to over $100,000; investigation, QA and instrumentation excluded
tables: Table 1-6: Comparative Unit Costs by Ground Modification Technology, November 2016
sections.applicability: Comparing typical unit costs of ground modification technologies.

sections.title: Preliminary Cost Estimation
sections.summary: Select on sound engineering first; initial cost should not drive the choice over performance, time, life-cycle cost, risk and safety. A preliminary estimate needs site information and a preliminary design for quantities; GeoTechTools provides cost spreadsheets for all technologies in the manual.
sections.body: Selection should be based first on sound engineering. When two or more technologies are technically feasible, initial cost is considered, but should not be the driving force: performance, construction time, life cycle costs, risks and safety should be factored in. A preliminary cost estimate needs site information, which also serves the preliminary design that gives quantities of materials and equipment. Guidance is in the technical summaries, and GeoTechTools (Section 7) provides Excel spreadsheets for preliminary estimates for all technologies in the manual. (p. 1-37)
key_points: Initial cost should not drive selection
Preliminary design gives the quantities for a preliminary estimate
GeoTechTools provides cost spreadsheets
sections.applicability: Preparing preliminary cost estimates for ground modification.

sections.title: GeoTechTools
sections.summary: GeoTechTools (geotechtools.org) is a web-based geoconstruction technology guidance and selection system, complementary to the manual, with a Users Guide on its home page.
sections.body: GeoTechTools is a web-based geoconstruction technologies guidance and selection system at http://www.geotechtools.org; the section reviews its development and content. The manual and GeoTechTools are complementary, and a Users Guide is available from the home page. (p. 1-38)
key_points: Web-based guidance and selection system, complementary to the manual
sections.applicability: Online resource for preliminary technology screening and case history research.

sections.title: Background, Development, Audience, and Use
sections.summary: GeoTechTools came from SHRP2 project R02 (renewal focus: rapid, minimal disruption, long-lived) on new embankments over unstable soils, widening and working platforms; it catalogs technologies, design, QC/QA, costs and specifications for agency engineers and others, organized in four applications (Figure 1-1).
sections.body: GeoTechTools was developed under SHRP2 (created by Congress in 2006; focus areas Safety, Renewal, Reliability, Capacity). Under Renewal, aimed at rapid, minimally disruptive, long-lived renewal, project R02 'Geotechnical Solutions for Soil Improvement, Rapid Embankment Construction, and Stabilization of the Pavement Working Platform' addressed new embankments and roadways over unstable soils, widening, and working platform stabilization. It identified existing and emerging technologies, implementation issues, performance criteria and QA/QC, and non-geotechnical obstacles, and assessed design, QC/QA, costs and specifications, cataloged in a web database. The audience is mainly public agency geotechnical staff, but others use it too (Schaefer et al. 2012). Final applications were the four areas of Figure 1-1, developed with the research team, an Advisory Board, an Expert Contact Group, FHWA and SHRP2. (pp. 1-38 to 1-39)
key_points: From SHRP2 project R02 (renewal: rapid, minimal disruption, long-lived)
Main audience: public agency geotechnical engineers
Organized in the four applications of Figure 1-1
sections.applicability: Origin and purpose of GeoTechTools.

sections.title: Catalog of Technologies
sections.summary: The Catalog of Technologies lists about 50 technologies, each with an information page rated for establishment in the U.S. and contribution to rapid renewal, minimal disruption and long life, linking fact sheets, photographs, case histories, design and QC/QA guidance, cost information, specifications and bibliography.
sections.body: The Catalog of Technologies lists the ~50 geoconstruction technologies, each linked to a Technology Information page with qualitative ratings: degree of establishment in the U.S. and potential contribution to rapid renewal, minimal traffic disruption and long-lived facilities. Each page links (mostly PDF) a Technology Fact Sheet, Photographs, Case Histories, Design Guidance, QC/QA Guidance, Cost Information, Specifications and Bibliography, based on assessments of advantages, disadvantages, soil types, depth and height limits, groundwater, materials, constraints, equipment and environment. (pp. 1-39 to 1-40)
key_points: About 50 technologies, each with ratings and eight documents
sections.applicability: Using the GeoTechTools technology catalog.

sections.title: Technology Selection Guidance
sections.summary: Technology Selection lists technologies by eleven classifications and offers an Interactive Selection Tool, a rule-based system starting from one of four applications; it does not replace the project geotechnical engineer, whose judgment weighs cost, maintenance, QC, performance, safety, inconvenience, environment and aesthetics.
sections.body: Technology Selection helps identify a targeted list of technologies for user-defined conditions (Douglas et al. 2012, 2014), by a listing sorted by classification and an Interactive Selection Tool; the information pages then support further screening (depth limits, soils, groundwater, project types, constraints, advantages and disadvantages). Classifications: earthwork construction, soft ground drainage and consolidation, densification of cohesionless soils, vertical support elements, embankments over soft soils, lateral earth support, cutoff walls, liquefaction mitigation, increased pavement performance, void filling, sustainability. The tool starts from one of four applications (construction over unstable soils; over stable or stabilized soils; pavement components; working platforms) and is a knowledge-based system of database tables and nested if-then rules. Results must be measured against the opinion of an experienced local geotechnical engineer; the tool does not replace the project Geotechnical Engineer, whose judgment weighs construction and maintenance cost, design and QC, performance and safety, inconvenience, environmental and aesthetic aspects. (pp. 1-40 to 1-41)
key_points: Eleven classifications plus a rule-based Interactive Selection Tool
The tool does not replace the project Geotechnical Engineer's judgment
sections.applicability: Using the GeoTechTools selection tool.

sections.title: Products/Tools
sections.summary: Each technology page gives eight products: fact sheet, photos, case histories, design guidance, QC/QA procedures, cost information with a preliminary cost spreadsheet (no rule-of-thumb costs; a preliminary design is needed first), specifications and a bibliography with a 22-category reference matrix.
sections.body: The eight products: a two-page Technology Fact Sheet (function, description, geologic applicability, construction, applications, complementary and alternate technologies, disadvantages, example applications, key references); Photos; two-page Case Histories, preferably U.S. state transportation agency projects (agencies are encouraged to add theirs); Design Guidance recommending an established procedure (e.g., an FHWA manual) or a preferred one, with considerations (performance criteria, subsurface, loading, materials, construction); QC/QA Procedures; Cost Information explaining cost items from specifications, with regional or bid-tab data where available, and a linked spreadsheet for preliminary estimates (not available for some technologies). Rule-of-thumb costs were avoided so technologies are not eliminated on cost alone; a valid cost comparison needs a preliminary design. A Specifications document (existing, newly developed, or topics to consider) and a Bibliography with a 22-category reference matrix. (pp. 1-41 to 1-42)
key_points: Eight products per technology
Cost spreadsheets need a preliminary design; no rule-of-thumb costs
Bibliography with a 22-category reference matrix
sections.applicability: GeoTechTools documents available for each technology.

sections.title: Summary
sections.summary: GeoTechTools collects information on over 50 geoconstruction and ground modification technologies in one place; built for transportation, it is useful to other civil construction industries.
sections.body: GeoTechTools is a web-based geoconstruction technologies guidance and selection system with information on over 50 technologies collected, synthesized, integrated and organized in a single location; developed for transportation, it can be equally valuable to other civil construction industries. (p. 1-42)
key_points: Over 50 technologies in one place
sections.applicability: Summary of GeoTechTools.

sections.title: Project Evaluation and Geotechnology Selection
sections.summary: Part 8.0 (pp. 1-43 to 1-52): the 12-step process for evaluating a project and selecting a ground modification technology, with a weighted selection matrix example and combinations of technologies.
sections.body: Heading of part 8.0, Project Evaluation and Geotechnology Selection; it has no text of its own before 8.1. Its sections introduce selection (8.1), set out the 12-step process (8.2), additional considerations (8.3), an example selection matrix (8.4) and combinations of technologies (8.5). (p. 1-43)
sections.applicability: Complete framework for systematic evaluation and selection of ground modification technologies for transportation projects.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Selecting and optimizing a ground modification method needs knowledge of feasible technologies, functions, selection criteria, design, QA, costs and environmental factors, applied in a logical sequence from simple to detailed so the best method emerges.
sections.body: Selecting a suitable ground modification method and optimizing its design and construction requires extensive knowledge of available and technically feasible technologies and careful evaluation of factors: functions, selection criteria, design procedures, QA methods, cost components and environmental factors. Evaluation should follow a logical, sequential process from simple to more detailed, allowing a best method to emerge. (p. 1-43)
key_points: A sequential process from simple to detailed lets the best method emerge
sections.applicability: Approach to selecting a ground modification technology.

sections.title: Process to Identify Potential Poor Ground Conditions and Need for Ground Modification
sections.summary: Table 1-7 lists the 12 selection steps: identify poor ground and need; performance requirements; general site conditions; subsurface conditions; short-list; constraints; risks; preliminary designs; alternative solutions; evaluate requirements, constraints and risks against selection factors; compare short-list; select.
sections.body: The process to identify potential poor ground, the need for ground modification and appropriate technologies follows a logical sequence, summarized in Table 1-7 and explained in 8.2.1 to 8.2.12: Step 1 identify potential poor ground conditions and need for ground modification; 2 identify or establish performance requirements; 3 identify and assess general site conditions; 4 assessment of subsurface conditions; 5 develop a short-list of geotechnologies applicable to site conditions; 6 consider project constraints; 7 consider project risks; 8 prepare a preliminary design; 9 identify alternative solutions (bridge, re-route, deep foundations, etc.); 10 evaluate project requirements, constraints and risks against factors affecting geotechnology selection; 11 compare the short-list with the selection factors; 12 select a preferred geotechnology. (p. 1-43)
key_points: Table 1-7: twelve geotechnology selection steps
tables: Table 1-7: Ground Modification Technology Selection Steps
sections.applicability: The 12-step ground modification technology selection process.

sections.title: Step 1: Identify Potential Poor Ground Conditions and Need for Ground Modification
sections.summary: Identify conditions that could require ground modification: poor ground (soft or loose soils causing immediate or long-term deformation or instability), constraints needing walls or steep slopes, pavement foundations, and equipment mobility needing a working platform.
sections.body: Identify project conditions that could require ground modification or geoconstruction: poor ground that will not adequately support a transportation structure (soft or loose foundation soils that under load would cause immediate or long-term deformation, or construction or post-construction instability); constraints requiring retaining walls or steep slopes; pavement foundations requiring improvement; construction equipment mobility issues requiring a working platform. (p. 1-44)
key_points: Poor ground, walls or steep slopes, pavement foundations, working platforms
sections.applicability: The 12-step ground modification technology selection process.

sections.title: Step 2: Identify or Establish Performance Requirements
sections.summary: Performance requirements include horizontal and vertical deformation limits, minimum stability factors of safety, improved nominal resistance, pavement stiffness, drainage, and available construction time.
sections.body: Performance requirements include deformation limits (horizontal and vertical), minimum factors of safety for stability, improved nominal resistance, stiffness parameters for pavements, drainage, and the available time for construction. (p. 1-44)
key_points: Deformation limits, stability factors of safety, resistance, stiffness, drainage, time
sections.applicability: The 12-step ground modification technology selection process.

sections.title: Step 3: Identify and Assess General Site Conditions
sections.summary: General site conditions are space (equipment access, storage, footprint and headroom), constructability and environmental constraints (spoil and dewatering water disposal, vibration, noise, dust), which in urban sites can rule out technologies.
sections.body: General site conditions consider space, constructability and environmental constraints. Space covers safe equipment access and on-site storage; urban congestion can affect operations and scheduling, and some technologies have large footprints and headroom needs. Environmental constraints include disposal of spoil (hazardous or not) and dewatering water, and construction vibrations, noise and dust, which in urban environments can rule out some technologies. (p. 1-44)
key_points: Footprint and headroom of the equipment matter
Urban vibration, noise and dust limits can rule out technologies
sections.applicability: The 12-step ground modification technology selection process.

sections.title: Step 4: Assess Subsurface Conditions
sections.summary: Identify the soils governing performance and their properties for preliminary design: at minimum type, depth, extent and groundwater; preferably shear strength and compressibility of poor soils; loads and deformation criteria help scope the investigation.
sections.body: The detail of subsurface assessment varies widely, but the soils affecting performance must be identified and their properties established for a preliminary design. At minimum the type, depth and extent and the groundwater table must be considered; for poor ground a preliminary assessment of shear strength and compressibility is valuable. Knowledge of the structure's loads and deformation criteria helps set the extent of investigation when particular techniques are under consideration. (pp. 1-44 to 1-45)
key_points: Minimum: type, depth, extent of poor soils and groundwater table
Shear strength and compressibility of poor soils
sections.applicability: The 12-step ground modification technology selection process.

sections.title: Step 5: Develop a Short-List of Geotechnologies Applicable to Site Conditions
sections.summary: A qualitative short-list considering performance criteria, subsurface limitations, schedule, environment and required improvement, from experience, this manual or the GeoTechTools Technology Selection.
sections.body: A short-list (preliminary selection) of applicable technologies is generally made qualitatively, considering the performance criteria, limitations from subsurface conditions, schedule and environmental constraints, and the level of improvement required, based on experience, this manual's guidance, or the Technology Selection part of GeoTechTools. (p. 1-45)
key_points: Qualitative short-list from experience, the manual or GeoTechTools
sections.applicability: The 12-step ground modification technology selection process.

sections.title: Step 6: Consider Project Constraints
sections.summary: Constraints affecting technology selection are considered in two groups, general (8.2.6.1) and geotechnical (8.2.6.2).
sections.body: Constraints that might affect the selection of ground modification technologies can be identified by considering general and geotechnical constraints (8.2.6.1 and 8.2.6.2). (p. 1-45)
sections.applicability: The 12-step ground modification technology selection process.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: General constraints (schedule, budget, right-of-way, geometry, utilities, traffic, weather, environment, agency staff and organization, contracting) include the delivery method's role; identifying as many as possible improves selection.
sections.body: General constraints include all items not connected with the geotechnical aspects: schedule and time; budget and cost; right-of-way limits, geometry, scale, utilities and sequence; traffic flow and interruption; weather; environmental; agency personnel, organization and structure; project management philosophy; and contracting processes. The project delivery method and its role in using these techniques should be assessed. Identifying as many constraints as possible allows better selection. (p. 1-45)
key_points: Assess the delivery method's effect on using these techniques
sections.applicability: The 12-step ground modification technology selection process.

sections.title: Geotechnical
sections.summary: Geotechnical constraints as in 4.1.2 (subsurface conditions, proprietary systems, experience, movements, stability, vibration, time to take effect, spoils, environment, contractors, constructability); the poor soils' types, depths, extent and properties are perhaps the most important.
sections.body: Geotechnical constraints are those specific to geotechnical aspects and candidate technologies: subsurface conditions including archaeological remains, contaminated groundwater, obstructions and buried utilities; proprietary products and processes; knowledge and experience; allowable vertical and horizontal movements; stability; noise and vibration; time for improvement to be effective; spoils development and disposal; environmental impacts; availability of qualified contractors, personnel, materials and specialty equipment; constructability. Identifying the poor soil types, depths, extent and engineering properties is perhaps the most important consideration. (pp. 1-45 to 1-46)
key_points: Poor soil types, depths, extent and properties: perhaps the most important
sections.applicability: The 12-step ground modification technology selection process.

sections.title: Step 7: Consider Project Risks
sections.summary: Risks from missed schedule and budget targets (contract issues, late notice to proceed, weather, access, materials, equipment), misidentified geotechnical issues, and a fix that does not work on the site soils; carry them forward from the investigation.
sections.body: Project risks arise from missing schedule and budget targets, misidentifying geotechnical issues, and providing an inappropriate or inadequate fix. Schedule and budget risks come from contractual issues between general and specialty contractors, a late notice to proceed, weather, site access, material supply and equipment availability, and must be continuously addressed. Geotechnical risks (slope instability, settlement, liquefaction, contamination, problem soils) should be identified in the subsurface investigation and carried forward. Selecting a method that turns out not to work in the site soils is also a risk. (p. 1-46)
key_points: Schedule, budget and geotechnical risks
A method that does not work in the site soils is itself a risk
sections.applicability: The 12-step ground modification technology selection process.

sections.title: Step 8: Prepare Preliminary Designs
sections.summary: Preliminary design of each candidate technology for the site, unique to its performance criteria and constraints, allows preliminary cost estimates to be developed and compared.
sections.body: From all the above, a preliminary list of suitable technologies is developed. To compare them, a preliminary design of each candidate for the site conditions must be completed, unique to the project performance criteria and constraints; preliminary cost estimates can then be developed and compared. (p. 1-46)
key_points: Preliminary design of each candidate, then compare preliminary costs
sections.applicability: The 12-step ground modification technology selection process.

sections.title: Step 9: Identify Alternative Solutions (Bridge, Re-route, Deep Foundations, etc.)
sections.summary: Alternative solutions, such as a bridge, deep foundations or rerouting around the poor ground, should always be evaluated alongside ground modification.
sections.body: Alternate solutions always exist and should be evaluated with the ground modification methods: a bridge system, deep foundations instead of ground modification, or rerouting the alignment to avoid the poor ground. (p. 1-46)
key_points: Evaluate a bridge, deep foundations or rerouting alongside
sections.applicability: The 12-step ground modification technology selection process.

sections.title: Step 10: Evaluate Project Requirements, Constraints, and Risks Against Factors Affecting Geotechnology Selection
sections.summary: Additional selection factors (constructability, speed, disruption, longevity, ROW, aesthetics, environment, familiarity, establishment, design procedure, contracting, initial and life-cycle cost, constraints, risks) each get a weight factor WF of 0 to 3, tabulated as in Table 1-8.
sections.body: Beyond the primary factors of Step 5 (application, purpose, soil types, depth), additional factors may include constructability (materials, equipment, staging, access, groundwater); speed of construction; construction disruption to the public and adjacent structures; longevity (service life, maintenance); ROW requirements; aesthetics; environmental concerns; local familiarity; degree of establishment; design procedure (availability, complexity, codified); contracting; cost (initial and life cycle); additional constraints; and project risks, which are evaluated explicitly. The list is not project specific; others may apply and many may not matter. The party responsible for selection (owner, its consultant or the contractor, depending on contracting) rates each factor's relevance with a weight factor (WF) from 0 to 3 (3 most relevant, 1 least, 0 or NA not relevant), tabulated as in Table 1-8. Speed, disturbance, longevity and cost are typically the most important 'wall selection factors for permanent wall systems' (as printed). (pp. 1-47 to 1-48)
key_points: Weight factor WF 0 to 3 for each selection factor
Table 1-8: geotechnology selection factors with WF 0 through 3
The selecting party depends on the contracting method
sections.applicability: The 12-step ground modification technology selection process.

sections.title: Step 11: Compare Short-List of Geotechnology Alternatives with Geotechnology Selection Factors
sections.summary: Each short-listed alternative gets a relative rating RR of 1 to 4 for how well it meets each selection factor, from experience with the technologies.
sections.body: Each short-listed alternative (Step 5) is rated against the selection factors with a relative rating (RR) from 1 to 4: four for the most suitable and one for the least suitable, based on experience with the short-listed geotechnologies in meeting the factors. (p. 1-48)
key_points: Relative rating RR 1 to 4 per factor and alternative
sections.applicability: The 12-step ground modification technology selection process.

sections.title: Step 12: Select a Preferred Geotechnology
sections.summary: In a selection matrix, weighted rating WR = WF x RR for each factor; the WRs sum to a Total Score and the highest becomes the base design, other high scorers acceptable alternates. The text takes WF 'from Table 1-7' (as printed; the weight factors are in Table 1-8).
sections.body: Alternatives are compared in a geotechnology selection matrix and the highest score is selected. For each factor the weighted rating WR is WF (the text says 'from Table 1-7', as printed; the weight factors are tabulated in Table 1-8) times the 1 to 4 relative rating; the WRs are added to a Total Score for each technology. The highest scoring technology should be developed as the base design; other high scorers may be included in the Contract Documents as acceptable alternates. An example is in Section 8.4. (pp. 1-48 to 1-49)
key_points: WR = WF x RR; Total Score = sum of WR
Highest score is the base design; other high scorers may be alternates
sections.applicability: The 12-step ground modification technology selection process.

sections.title: Additional Considerations - Detailed Subsurface Investigation, Design, and Cost Estimate
sections.summary: After selection, supplemental detailed subsurface investigation may be needed for the specialized geomaterial parameters of final design and cost estimate; the technology summaries give the parameters.
sections.body: Once a geotechnology is selected, more information may be needed for final design and cost estimate. Ground modification often needs specialized geomaterial parameters not obtained in preliminary investigations, so supplemental detailed subsurface investigations are sometimes necessary; the technology summaries detail the parameters. (p. 1-49)
key_points: Selected technologies may need supplemental, specialized investigation
sections.applicability: Work after selecting a ground modification technology.

sections.title: Geotechnology Selection Example
sections.summary: Table 1-9 is a sample selection matrix of three technologies over 16 factors: totals 75 (A), 69 (B) and 64 (C), so A goes to final design and B may be an alternate. As printed, the constructability row gives WR 3 for WF 3 x RR 2 (A and B), and B's printed total 69 is one more than its column sum.
sections.body: Selection factors differ for each project. Table 1-9 is a sample matrix (weight factor; relative and weighted ratings for Geotech A, B, C): speed of construction 2; minimize disturbance 2; longevity 3; cost of construction 2; constructability 3; ROW NA; aesthetics NA; environmental 1; degree of establishment 3; familiarity 2; design procedure 2; contracting 1; life-cycle cost 1; constraint - construction season 3; risk - delay due to settlement time 3; risk - quality assurance 2. Total scores: A 75, B 69, C 64. Weight factors come from Step 10 and Table 1-8, relative ratings from Step 11, and the total is the sum of weighted ratings; A would advance to final design and cost analysis and B may be accepted as an alternate. As printed, the constructability row gives weighted ratings 3, 3 and 6 for relative ratings 2, 2 and 2 at WF 3, and B's weighted ratings add to 68 against the printed 69. (pp. 1-49 to 1-51)

Highest total (A) to final design; B may be an alternate
As printed: constructability WR 3 for 3 x 2 (A, B); B column sums to 68, printed 69

sections.title: Combination of Geotechnologies
sections.summary: Combinations of technologies should be considered: e.g., shallow compaction above blast densification's untreated upper 5 ft, PVDs with fill preloading, lightweight fill on column supported embankments, or different methods where conditions vary. Table 1-10 marks combinations found in a literature review (Barngrover et al. 2013).
sections.body: Combinations should be considered in selection; typical ones are in each technology summary's complementary technology section and the GeoTechTools fact sheets. Of many possible combinations (Table 1-10), some are more likely to succeed: blast densification does not densify the upper 5 feet, which can be compacted by a shallow method such as rapid impact compaction; PVDs and fill preloading together accelerate consolidation and schedule; lightweight fill reduces load on column supported embankments; and varying subsurface conditions may warrant different technologies across a project. Table 1-10 marks combinations with case histories found in a literature review on embankments over unstable ground (Barngrover et al. 2013) among PVDs and fill preloading, vacuum preloading, vibro-compaction, deep dynamic compaction, blast densification, aggregate columns, geotextile encased columns, deep mixing, jet grouting, soil nailing, MSE walls, reinforced soil slopes, lightweight fills, column supported embankments and micropiles (blank cells: no case history located). (pp. 1-51 to 1-52)
key_points: Blast densification leaves the upper 5 ft untreated; add shallow compaction
PVDs with fill preloading; lightweight fill on column supported embankments
Table 1-10: combinations found in literature (Barngrover et al. 2013)
